title: Human resource management strategy
overview: HRM strategy connects workforce decisions to long-term performance. You must compare hard and soft HRM, evaluate flexible contracts, diagnose and improve employee performance, understand Management by Objectives (MBO), and analyse how IT/AI changes HRM.
syllabusPoints: Evaluate flexible working contracts and arrangements.
Measure causes/consequences of poor employee performance and recommend improvements.
Explain implementation and usefulness of MBO.
Analyse the changing role of IT and AI in HRM.
Design a coherent HR policy bundle that fits business objectives and diagnoses performance evidence.
Interpret changes in employee-performance measures, including percentage-point changes.

definitions.definition: An approach treating labour mainly as a resource/cost to be planned and controlled to meet business needs.
An approach treating employees as assets whose commitment, development and participation create performance.
Management by Objectives: managers and employees agree measurable objectives, monitor progress and review results.
Employment arrangements allowing labour time/location/contract to adapt to employee or business needs.
A contract specifying total hours for the year, with working time varied between periods to match demand.
Working normal weekly hours over fewer, longer days.
A labour market in which individuals complete short tasks or contracts, often arranged through digital platforms.
A structured review of employee performance, development needs and future objectives.

sections.title: Hard versus soft HRM
content: Hard HRM emphasises workforce numbers, productivity and cost; soft HRM emphasises motivation, development, trust and involvement. Real firms may combine both. The suitable balance depends on skill scarcity, service quality, cost pressure, business objectives and culture.

An HR strategy is a connected policy bundle, not a label. Recruitment, contracts, training, rewards, job design and employee relations should reinforce the same objective; conflicting policies can cancel one another.
bullets: A hard approach can match labour cost and numbers quickly to demand, but insecurity may reduce discretionary effort, retention and service quality.
A soft approach can build firm-specific skill and commitment, but training, consultation and secure contracts create cost and take time to pay back.
A hospital may use hard workforce budgets and strict safety measures while using soft development and participation to retain scarce nurses.

examples.label: A conflicting policy bundle
examples.content: A hotel promises empowerment and service training but gives staff insecure shifts and rewards only the number of rooms cleaned. The hard controls may undermine the trust and quality behaviour the soft policies were meant to create.

sections.title: Flexible contracts and working
content: Temporary, zero-hours, part-time, full-time, annualised hours, flexitime, home working, shifts, job sharing, compressed hours and gig work allow labour to match demand or widen recruitment. Risks include insecurity, coordination difficulty, legal and reputation issues and weaker loyalty or training continuity.

Contract flexibility changes the quantity of labour available; working-time and location flexibility change when or where employees work. The same arrangement can benefit both sides, or transfer all demand risk to workers, depending on notice, choice, pay and access to development.

Flexitime lets employees vary start and finish times around agreed core hours. It can widen recruitment and reduce lateness where workers have caring or travel constraints, but customer coverage, team coordination and supervision become harder unless rotas guarantee required staffing.

Shift working divides extended or 24-hour operations into scheduled periods. It raises asset use and provides continuous customer coverage in hospitals, factories or transport, but night premiums, fatigue and poor handovers can increase cost, errors and safety risk.

Job sharing lets two employees split one full-time role. It can retain experienced workers and provide continuity when one partner is absent, but handover failures, duplicated communication and unclear accountability can damage service; it best suits work that can be divided with reliable records.
bullets: Annualised hours move labour toward seasonal peaks but can create fatigue or overtime cost if hours are allocated badly.
Compressed hours reduce commuting days and may improve retention, but longer shifts can harm concentration, safety or customer coverage.
Gig work gives rapid access to capacity and specialist skill, but control, employment status, quality and availability may be uncertain.
Home working widens recruitment and may reduce office cost, yet requires outcome measures, secure systems and deliberate team communication.

sections.title: Measuring poor performance
content: Indicators include productivity, absence, labour turnover, error and defect rates, complaints and missed targets. Causes may be skill gaps, poor equipment, unclear goals, workload, weak motivation, leadership or reward systems. Diagnose the cause before choosing a solution.

Measures show symptoms, not proof of cause. Compare time trends, departments and benchmarks, then use appraisal, exit interviews, observation and employee feedback to separate ability, motivation, resources and external-demand effects.
bullets: If absence rises from 4% to 6%, it increases by 2 percentage points, or 50% relative to the original rate; state which comparison is used.
Higher labour productivity can reflect automation or fewer workers, not necessarily better employee performance.
Low turnover is not always good if weak performers remain and the business needs new skills; high turnover is most damaging where replacement and learning costs are high.

sections.title: Improving performance
content: Training, coaching, better job design, participation, clearer targets, technology, reward changes, wellbeing support or better recruitment may help. Evaluate cost, implementation time and whether the problem is individual or systemic.

Match the policy to diagnosis: training addresses an ability gap, clearer objectives address ambiguity, maintenance addresses equipment failure and job redesign or fair rewards may address motivation. Review several measures so one target is not improved by damaging quality or wellbeing.
bullets: Appraisal can identify development needs and provide feedback, but biased ratings or a punishment-only meeting reduce trust.
Participation can reveal process constraints and improve acceptance, but needs real authority and management response.
Performance-related pay can focus effort on measurable output but may encourage gaming, short-termism or weak teamwork.

sections.title: Management by Objectives
content: Managers and employees agree objectives aligned with higher business goals, measures and timescales, then review progress. Benefits include clarity, participation, alignment and performance evidence. Risks include target gaming, narrow focus, measurement difficulty and time spent negotiating and reviewing.

Implementation cascades the corporate objective into departmental and individual SMART objectives, agrees resources and authority, monitors milestones, gives feedback and reviews results. Employees should understand how their target contributes to the wider objective.
bullets: Participation can improve realism and commitment, especially where employees know the process better than senior managers.
Objectives must cover quality, customer and team effects as well as easy quantity measures.
MBO becomes bureaucratic when targets stay fixed after conditions change or review focuses on blame rather than learning.

sections.title: IT and AI in HRM
content: Systems automate applicant screening, scheduling, payroll, training and performance analytics. Benefits include speed and consistency; risks include algorithmic bias, privacy, cybersecurity, inaccurate data and loss of human judgement and trust.

AI can predict turnover, match candidates, personalise training and answer routine employee queries. It changes HR work toward data interpretation, exception handling, employee experience and governance rather than removing the need for human judgement.
bullets: Historical recruitment data may encode past discrimination, so apparently neutral screening can reproduce bias at scale.
Employees need transparency, access controls, correction routes and human review for consequential decisions.
Automation can release HR time and improve consistency, but system cost, poor data, cyber failure and employee surveillance concerns may offset the gain.

formulas.label: Labour productivity
formulas.expression: Output in a period ÷ number of employees
formulas.note: Use labour hours instead of employees if the question specifies hours.

formulas.label: Labour turnover
formulas.expression: (Employees leaving in a period ÷ average number employed) × 100

formulas.label: Percentage-point change
formulas.note: A change from 4% to 6% is 2 percentage points, but a 50% relative increase.

nodes: Keep, adapt or stop the policy

analysisChains.title: Soft HRM investment
steps: Labour turnover and recruitment costs may fall
analysisChains.evaluation: Benefits depend on retaining trained staff and measuring whether performance gains exceed the programme's cost.

analysisChains.title: Annualised hours for seasonal demand
steps: More contracted hours are scheduled during the peak season
Overtime and idle-time cost may fall
analysisChains.evaluation: Forecast error can exhaust annual hours too early, while unpopular schedules can increase fatigue, absence and turnover.

analysisChains.title: AI applicant screening
steps: The system compares many applications against job criteria quickly
Recruitment time and administrative cost fall
Capacity and customer service recover faster
analysisChains.evaluation: Biased historic data or a weak criterion can exclude strong candidates at scale; audit, transparency and human review are necessary.

analysisChains.title: Management by Objectives
steps: Corporate objectives are translated into agreed employee targets
Employees understand priorities and how performance is measured
Effort and coordination focus on the objective
Progress data allows earlier corrective action
Productivity or service performance may improve
analysisChains.evaluation: Narrow or unrealistic targets encourage gaming and stress; measures and objectives need review when conditions change.

examTips: Flexible working is not automatically soft HRM—the motive and employee treatment matter.
If performance is poor, connect the solution to the actual cause.
AI evaluation should include bias/data/privacy risk as well as efficiency.
For an overall HR strategy, show how policies reinforce or contradict one another before reaching a judgement.
commonMistakes: Treating part-time and temporary as the same.
Recommending training when poor equipment/targets are the real cause.
Describing MBO as only top-down target setting.

quickRecall.question: How do hard and soft HRM differ?
quickRecall.answer: Hard HRM treats labour mainly as a controllable resource and cost; soft HRM develops employees as assets and partners.

quickRecall.question: What are annualised hours?
quickRecall.answer: A yearly total of contracted hours allocated unevenly across periods to match demand.

quickRecall.question: What is a percentage-point change?
quickRecall.answer: The arithmetic difference between two percentages, such as 6% minus 4% = 2 percentage points.

quickRecall.question: What is the first step when performance is poor?
quickRecall.answer: Diagnose the cause using trends, benchmarks and qualitative evidence before choosing a policy.

quickRecall.question: How is MBO implemented?
quickRecall.answer: Align agreed measurable objectives from corporate to individual level, provide resources, monitor progress and review results.

quickRecall.question: What is a central risk of AI in HRM?
quickRecall.answer: Biased or inaccurate data can make unfair decisions at scale, alongside privacy and trust risks.
